## Introduction

The term "foundation model" entered the AI lexicon around 2021, coined by researchers at Stanford to describe large neural networks trained on vast, diverse datasets that can be adapted — through fine-tuning or prompting — to a wide range of downstream tasks. GPT-4, Gemini, and Claude are foundation models for language. The defining characteristic is not their size alone, but the breadth of their pretraining: they learn general representations of their domain that transfer efficiently to specialized problems. Earth observation foundation models (EOFMs) apply this logic to satellite and aerial imagery. Rather than training a separate model from scratch for each task, such as flood detection or crop classification, an EO foundation model attempts to produce general-purpose representations. Their assumption is that such shared backbones can then be adapted to downstream applications with relatively little labeled data.

In `sits`, we are particularly interested in building EOFMs using satellite image time series. Many EOFMa treat each image as an independent observation — a frozen snapshot of the world at a single moment. But the planet is not static, and some of its most important signals are written not in any single image but in how a place changes over time. A foundation model built on satellite image time series takes that temporal dimension as a basis, treating sequences of observations as the primary unit of learning.


## Building foundational models

In a general sense, an "Earth observation foundation model" (EOFM) is a neural network architectures that 
has been trained on large unlabeled datasets using self-supervised learning (SSL) strategies. SSL works by setting an optimization criteria (the so-called self-supervision). Alarge amount of unlabeled data is then used to train a model by optimizing this objective without requiring any manual annotation. Given a carefully designed self-supervised problem, the model f gets the ability to capture high-level representations of the input data. Afterward, the model can be further transferred to supervised downstream tasks [@Wang2022a].

Most current EO foundation models (FM) borrow their architecture from computer vision: the Vision Transformer, or ViT, has become a dominant backbone. Images are divided into patches, each patch is embedded as a token, and a transformer learns relationships among those tokens across the full scene. The pretraining objective is typically masked image modelling — patches are hidden, and the model must reconstruct them from context — which forces it to learn meaningful scene structure rather than surface statistics.

In `sits`, we work differently, treating a time series of images as a sequence of tokens and learning how scenes evolve. 
Rather than feeding the model on image patches, the input is a collection of time series. The same geographic locations are captured repeatedly over months or years, at regular intervals. Each acquisition in the stack becomes a temporal token. The model's job during pretraining is to learn what makes the sequence coherent — the rhythms, transitions, and anomalies that distinguish a wheat field from a pine forest, a growing city from a stable one, a drying lake from a healthy one.

A fraction of the time series — randomly selected time steps — are masked out, and the model must reconstruct them from the unmasked context. This is deceptively powerful: to accurately predict a missing patch in late summer, the model must have learned something real about vegetation phenology, shadow geometry, soil reflectance, and the typical progression of a growing season at that latitude.

The deeper insight behind this class of models is that time is a label. A model forced to predict masked observations within a coherent time series will be able to represent the underlying physical and ecological processes that generate that coherence — the phenology, the hydrology, the urban dynamics. That representation is not based on training data; it is induced from the data itself. Thus, a FM learns the fundamental physical, spatial, and temporal rules of the Earth’s surface by finding patterns in the data. 

In `sits` we use masked autoencoders (MAE) for semi-supervised learning. The model is fed a satellite image time series where a large portion (often up to 75%) of the values has been masked. The model aims to reconstruct the missing values based on the available values. To do this successfully, the model must learn what features naturally co-occur in the real world. When processing  time-series data, the EOFM learns the temporal signatures of land cover and land use pixels. 

## What is an embedding?

In traditional remote sensing, a geographic location is represented by an array of pixel values across time and space. These pixel values are multidimensional.  When this raw data is passed through an EO Foundational Model, the neural network compresses and transforms it into an "embedding" — a dense, high-dimensional numerical vector (often 64, 128, or 768 dimensions). This embedding acts as a mathematical summary of that specific location.

After pretraining on millions of location-time series, one expects model's embeddings to capture different kinds of information:

* Phenological state — where in the growth cycle a parcel of vegetation is, independent of the calendar date
* Land cover type — forest, cropland, wetland, built-up area, bare soil, water — discriminated by the shape of the time series rather than any single image
* Change regime — gradual trends (slow urbanisation, progressive deforestation), seasonal cycles (agriculture, snowpack), and abrupt events (fire, flood, construction)
* Anomaly signatures — deviations from the expected seasonal trajectory that may indicate stress, disturbance, or human activity

## Global and local embeddings

Foundation models are not panaceas. Pretraining data shapes what a model can and cannot know: a model trained predominantly on temperate agricultural landscapes may generalize poorly to tropical forests or Arctic tundra. Evaluation benchmarks are still maturing, and it is not always clear how to measure genuine geospatial understanding as opposed to texture memorization.
